2027 budget: in the Senate, the right wants €6 billion more in savings, an end to the pensioners' tax allowance and only one in two retiring civil servants replaced

On Friday, November 20, the Senate began examining the 2027 state budget, which MPs had rejected. Facing more than 3,000 amendments, the right-wing and centrist majority wants to increase the effort by about €6 billion, notably by scrapping the 10% allowance on pensions, which would bring in €4.7 billion [1][3][5].
The bill, sent to the Senate on November 19, is being examined starting with revenue, from November 20 to 28 or 29, then spending, from November 30 to December 9 [1].
It is the government's original version that is arriving: MPs rejected the revenue section on November 4 by 458 votes to 0, wiping out their amendments [8].
More than 3,000 amendments have been tabled on the revenue section alone [5].

General rapporteur Christine Lavarde proposes scrapping the 10% allowance for professional expenses on retirement pensions, worth €4.7 billion in 2027 [3]. The Senate majority also wants to replace only one in two civil servants who retire [3].
For local authorities, the Senate wants to bring the effort required down to “between €2 and €2.5 billion” [6].

The bill forecasts 1.8% growth in 2027, debt at 121.7% of GDP and debt interest costs of €91.2 billion, compared with €79.2 billion in 2026 [2]. It extends the surtax on large companies by one year, reduced by 30% [2], and makes half of the daily sickness benefits of patients with long-term illnesses taxable [9].
On the left, Communist senators accuse the right of wanting to “amplify fiscal and social injustices” [7].
Key takeaway: the Senate, dominated by the right and the centre, is rewriting a budget that the National Assembly rejected unanimously, and it is toughening it rather than softening it [3][8].

The heart of the problem is debt: its cost, meaning the interest paid each year, would rise by €12 billion in one year, to €91.2 billion [2]. This is the Senate majority's argument for demanding more savings [3].

The timetable is tight: the Senate's formal vote is scheduled for December 9 and the deadline is set for December 17 [8]. Without agreement with the National Assembly, the government must choose between Article 49.3, ordinances or a compromise, each of which exposes it to a no-confidence motion [10].
Pensioners are on the front line: with €4.7 billion expected, ending the 10% allowance would be the largest revenue measure proposed by the Senate majority [3].

If you are a retiree who pays income tax, scrapping the 10% allowance would increase your taxable income, and therefore your tax. If you are an employee, indexing the income tax brackets to inflation, as planned in the bill, prevents an automatic increase [2]. Nothing has been voted yet: everything will be decided in December.

China-Australia: Xi Jinping hails a “complete turnaround” in front of Albanese, but nothing is settled on iron ore, beef or the port of Darwin

On Friday, November 20, in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of APEC, Xi Jinping hailed a “complete turnaround” in Sino-Australian relations in front of Anthony Albanese. That evening in Beijing, the Australian leader and Premier Li Qiang launched a dialogue on artificial intelligence. Nothing was settled on iron ore, beef or the port of Darwin [1][4][8].

According to the Chinese Foreign Ministry, Xi Jinping wants the two countries to be “partners who trust each other” and proposes cooperation in agriculture, energy, minerals, digital technology and AI. 2027 will be the “Australia-China Year of Tourism” [2].

For Anthony Albanese, it was his fifth bilateral meeting with Xi Jinping, according to his office's transcript. He described it as “constructive, friendly” and in the “mutual interest” of both countries [3]. Australia must “manage its differences” with China “without being defined by them,” he added [1].

Iron ore weighed on the meeting. The Chinese state buyer China Mineral Resources Group (CMRG) pools purchases to obtain better terms and this year restricted some purchases from BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue [6][7]. BHP and Rio Tinto have since signed new contracts, while Fortescue is still negotiating [6].

Another point of friction is beef: China's import quota of 205,000 tonnes was reached as early as June, triggering a 55% customs duty beyond that [4][5]. Canberra is also demanding that the Chinese company Landbridge give up its lease on the port of Darwin; the company does not rule out international legal action [1][5].

That evening in Beijing, Anthony Albanese and Chinese Premier Li Qiang agreed to create a dialogue on the safety, governance and uses of AI, as part of their annual meeting [8][9]. No date or format has been published [9].

At the 9th roundtable of business leaders from both countries, where 11 executives were expected, including those of BHP and Rio Tinto, companies called for better access to the Chinese market for beef, wheat and rice, without concrete progress [7][8][9].

Key takeaway: China and Australia have closed the pre-2022 crisis, when Beijing blocked several Australian products that are now allowed again, but their relationship remains a commercial power struggle, above all over iron ore [1][8].

By entrusting its ore purchases to a single state-owned company, Beijing is seeking to influence prices against the Australian mining giants. Canberra has warned that these centralised purchases threaten prices and government revenue [6].

The AI dialogue shows the balance Australia is seeking: it comes just after a declaration signed with the United States, partly to reduce dependence on critical Chinese technologies [9]. “We want to shape the future of AI, not be shaped by it,” Anthony Albanese summed up [9].
Security issues remain open: the screening of Chinese investment in critical minerals and the port of Darwin, whose return Albanese does not guarantee before the 2028 elections [1][5].

Australian iron ore is used to make Chinese steel, which ends up in cars and machinery sold in Europe. If Beijing gets cheaper ore, its exported steel can become cheaper too, increasing pressure on European steelmakers.

news.2026-11-21-gaza-frappes-incursion-b: Gaza: six killed in Israeli strikes the day after the first ground incursion since the ceasefire

On Friday, November 20, Israeli strikes killed six people in the Gaza Strip, according to the civil defence, the day after the end of a tank incursion into the centre of the territory, beyond the ceasefire's “yellow line.” The Board of Peace warns that the truce is no longer moving forward [1][3][4].

According to Mahmoud Bassal, spokesperson for Gaza's civil defence (a rescue service under Hamas), four people were killed on Friday in an airstrike southwest of the Bureij camp. Two others died in drone strikes, one in a displacement camp in Deir al-Balah, the other north of Nuseirat [1][2].

The Israeli army says it “targeted several fighters” in these strikes [1]. The day before, it had announced the end of its ground operation in central Gaza and the reopening of Salah al-Din Road [1][5].

On Wednesday, November 18, tanks and bulldozers crossed the “yellow line,” which separates the area held by Israel from the one held by Hamas, heading towards the road between the Nuseirat and Bureij camps [5]. It was the first ground push since the start of the ceasefire [3].

The operation affected about 2.5 km² where more than 18,000 people lived, according to an initial analysis by the UN humanitarian office (OCHA) [1][3]. The army ordered residents of three blocks to leave their shelters [5].

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said he was “fully prepared to seize more territory, to evacuate residents,” adding that the land taken would become “permanent parts of Israel's security zones” [6].
In early November, Gaza's Health Ministry counted 1,602 Palestinians killed since the ceasefire took effect in October 2025, and 74,618 since the start of the war in October 2023 [7].

Key takeaway: the truce in Gaza is holding less and less. This week's incursion shows that Israel is ready to advance beyond the line set by the agreement, and its defence minister talks of keeping this land permanently [3][6].

The Board of Peace, the body tasked with overseeing the plan for Gaza, wrote to the UN Security Council that Israel and Hamas were not honouring their key commitments. As a result, the new Palestinian administration and the international security force provided for by the agreement are delayed [4].

The report also criticises Israel for failing to take the decisions needed to train and deploy a Palestinian civilian police force meant to replace Hamas [4]. Without this police force or an international force, the yellow line remains the only border, and it is moving [4][5].

Gaza may seem far away, but the failure of the ceasefire weighs on the whole region, already at war around Iran, and on debates in France and Europe about humanitarian aid and relations with Israel. If you want to follow what happens next, the date to remember is the presentation of the report to the UN at the end of November.

Japan: Takaichi will meet the ICC president sanctioned by Washington on Tuesday, and Tokyo will pay its 2027 contribution early to support the Court

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi will receive Tomoko Akane, president of the International Criminal Court (ICC), who was sanctioned by the United States in August, in Tokyo on Tuesday, November 24. According to the Jiji news agency, Japan also plans to pay its 2027 contribution in advance, to help the Court, which is at risk of being cut off from the dollar [1][2][3].

The Jiji agency reported on November 20 that Sanae Takaichi will receive Tomoko Akane on Tuesday at her office in Tokyo. It will be their first meeting since Donald Trump's administration placed the ICC president on its sanctions list in August [1][2].

According to the same source, Tokyo plans to pay its mandatory 2027 contribution to the ICC in advance [1][2]. As recently as November 12, government spokesperson Minoru Kihara said nothing had been decided [3].

In October, Washington sanctioned the Court itself, with a 180-day grace period. If these sanctions apply in full, the ICC could be cut off from dollar payments, threatening its operations, down to paying its staff's salaries [3][4].

Japan usually pays its share after April. This year it paid about ¥4.6 billion, the largest contribution of any member country. The advance could be included in a second supplementary budget for fiscal year 2026 [3][4].

This announcement comes the day after a difficult APEC summit for Sanae Takaichi: in Shenzhen, she did not obtain a real one-on-one with Xi Jinping [5]. She repeated that Japan's position on Taiwan had not changed, citing the 1972 China-Japan Joint Communiqué [6].

After the summit, she spoke for about twenty minutes with Donald Trump about the Indo-Pacific and Ukraine [7]. On November 20, she also met Chilean President José Antonio Kast: the two countries want to strengthen their cooperation on defence and critical minerals [8].
Key takeaway: Japan, one of the United States' closest allies, is choosing to openly support a Court that Washington is sanctioning, a rare divergence in their relationship [1][3].

US sanctions strike through the dollar: an institution cut off from dollar payments struggles to pay suppliers and employees, because banks fear being sanctioned in turn. By paying its contribution earlier, Tokyo gives the Court cash before the end of the 180-day grace period [3][4].

For Sanae Takaichi, the balance is delicate: she spoke with Donald Trump right after the summit and is careful with her ally, while defending international law [7]. Snubbed by Beijing, she could, on the other hand, gain from it with her most loyal base, according to analysts cited by AFP [5].

Dollar sanctions show the power of the US currency: even an international court based in Europe can be paralysed if it loses access to the dollar. It is the same lever Washington can use against European banks or companies. If Japan, the ICC's largest contributor, supports it, the Court gains time.

news.2026-11-21-sri-lanka-budget-2027-gr: Colombo, Sri Lanka
Sri Lanka
Sri Lanka: the budget for exiting the IMF programme clears Parliament on the day 20 civil service unions called a strike

On Friday, November 20, Sri Lanka's Parliament passed the 2027 budget at second reading by 157 votes to 60. This budget is meant to accompany the end of the IMF programme in March 2027. On the same day, 20 unions of senior civil servants called a national strike against allowance increases they consider unfair [1][2][3][8].

The budget was passed with a majority of 97 votes, after seven days of debate. It had been presented by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, who is also Minister of Finance [1][2]. The clause-by-clause examination begins on November 21 and the final vote is scheduled for December 14 at 6 p.m. [1][2].

The bill provides for 7,933 billion rupees in spending, 6,180 billion in revenue and grants, and a deficit of 1,753 billion rupees, or 4.5% of GDP [7]. It is the third budget of the National People's Power (NPP) government [7].

The IMF's four-year programme, the “Extended Fund Facility” that frames the country's finances, is due to end in March 2027. Anura Kumara Dissanayake announced that a special government committee would study whether to request a new programme [8]. The budget aims for growth that goes beyond a simple post-crisis recovery [8].

The joint committee of senior public servants had called a one-day nationwide strike on November 20, involving 20 unions [3][4][9]. It accuses the government of raising allowances for some categories of senior officials while forgetting the other 20 [4].

The anger goes beyond these officials: since November 16, several public-sector unions have launched actions against the budget [5]. The Ceylon Teachers' Union criticises the bill for not funding the remaining two-thirds of the promised catch-up between teachers' salaries and those of school principals [5].

Agriculture Minister K. D. Lalkantha replied that people would have to wait for the next budget: the 2027 one does not include a new increase to align public salaries with the cost of living [6]. Government spokesperson Nalinda Jayatissa promises to examine the demands once the budget has been passed [5].
Key takeaway: Sri Lanka is preparing to exit the IMF programme without loosening budgetary discipline, and civil servants are demanding their share [6][8].

The government is caught in a vice. If it raises public salaries, it widens an already rising deficit; if it does nothing, discontent spreads to government offices and schools, just when it wants to prove to the markets and the IMF that the country can stand on its own [5][7][8].

With 157 votes out of 217 cast, President Dissanayake's majority remains solid in Parliament [1]. But the officials' strike, the teachers' anger and the minister's response, which pushes everything back to the following budget, show that social patience is wearing thin [4][5][6].

Sri Lanka is a popular destination for European travellers. Exiting the IMF programme without a new crisis is the condition for the country to remain stable and for its prices and currency not to spiral as they did during the crisis. If you travel there, strikes in government offices may slow down some procedures, but for now the movement is limited to days of action.

France
Abivax loses 17% in Paris: a US fund bets on its fall and accuses the French biotech of “fraud” over its flagship drug

On Friday, November 20, shares in French biotech Abivax fell more than 17% in Paris, after a report by US fund Scorpion Capital, which is short-selling the stock. It questions the safety of obefazimod, the company's treatment for ulcerative colitis. Abivax denounces the claims as “inaccurate and misleading” [1][2][4].

In Paris, Abivax fell about 17%, to €63, according to Zonebourse [2]; ABC Bourse reports a drop of more than 17% at the close [1]. In New York, where the company is also listed, the stock ended down about 9% [5].
The report by Scorpion Capital, a fund specialising in “activist” short selling, is titled “A Biotech Fraud For The Ages” [1][6].

The fund claims that obefazimod dissolves in fat in the same way as banned pesticides, which Abivax allegedly did not disclose, and that laboratory tests suggest a light-related cancer risk [6]. It also cites 17 recorded cancer cases, 16 of them in treated patients, and a low share of North American patients in the trials [7].

Scorpion acknowledges that it is short-selling the stock and says it intends to buy back a large part of its position as soon as the report is published: it therefore makes money from the decline [6].
As of November 17, about 6.25% of Abivax's share capital was already subject to short positions held by several funds, according to Zonebourse [2].

In the evening, Abivax responded that the report contains numerous “factually inaccurate and misleading” claims, highlighted Scorpion's financial interest in a decline and announced a thorough review [4].
The company says it still plans to file its approval application with the FDA, the US drug regulator, by the end of the year [4].

Key takeaway: a biotech that does not yet have an approved drug is worth what investors believe about its single product. Any attack on the safety of obefazimod therefore directly hits the entire value of the company [3].

Short selling is legal, and its defenders say it uncovers fraud. But the fund that publishes the report earns more the further the stock falls, which pushes it to hit hard; its accusations have not been independently verified at this stage [6].
The real judge will be the FDA: if the application filed by the end of the year convinces the agency, the attack will remain an episode; otherwise, the report will have been a warning sign [4].

Abivax is one of the few French biotechs to have become stock market stars, closely followed by retail investors. This session is a reminder that a stock that depends on a single drug can lose a sixth of its value in one day, on mere accusations that have not yet been settled.

How it works: “activist” short selling

Short selling means borrowing shares to sell them immediately, then buying them back later to return them. If the price has fallen in the meantime, you pocket the difference. An “activist” short seller goes further: it takes its position, then publishes a damning report to convince the market that the stock is worth much less. Scorpion says it intends to buy back a large part of its shares as soon as the report is published [6], in other words, to cash in its gain during the fall. The targeted company usually responds with a denial and, sometimes, legal action.
Precedents: from Abivax's surge to Scorpion's attacks
Abivax announces positive results from two phase 3 trials involving 1,275 patients with ulcerative colitis; its stock jumps more than 400% before the New York open, according to RTTNews [8].
Abivax's value rests almost entirely on obefazimod: that is what makes it so sensitive to both good and bad news.

news.2026-11-21-allemagne-fruhstartrente: Germany: the state will pay €10 a month into a securities account for every child, starting in January 2027

On Friday, November 20, the Bundesrat, the chamber representing the Länder, approved the “Frühstartrente,” an “early start” pension. The state will pay €10 a month, from age 6 to 18, into an account held in the name of every child born from 2020 onwards. The first payments begin on January 1, 2027 [1][2].
The scheme covers children born from 2020 onwards and resident in Germany. For children born in 2020, the support is backdated to January 1, 2026 [2].
Ten euros a month for twelve years adds up to €1,440 paid by the state per child, excluding investment returns [2].
The money must be invested in a securities account modelled on the standard product of the reformed private pension, taken out online and without mandatory advice [3].
The Bundestag had passed the bill in October [3][4].
Key takeaway: Germany is counting on the stock market to supplement tomorrow's pensions, and the right (CDU-CSU) hopes this will develop a culture of share ownership and investment in companies [3].

Criticism focuses on fairness: the Greens denounce a “two-tier” system, because parents and grandparents can top up the account [4], and consumer associations point out that it is the parents who have to choose and open the product [5].

Nothing like this exists in France for now, but the debate over a funded component in pensions comes up regularly. The German experiment will give an idea of what a small regular payment invested over decades can yield.

news.2026-11-21-perou-seisme-junin.title: Peru: a magnitude 6.7 earthquake shakes the Andes and sends Lima residents into the streets, a hospital cracked
news.2026-11-21-perou-seisme-junin.summa: A magnitude 6.7 earthquake struck central Peru on Friday, November 20, at 7:09 p.m. local time, 30 kilometres northwest of the town of Junín. It was felt as far away as Lima; no casualties had been reported as of Saturday [1][2][3].
news.2026-11-21-perou-seisme-junin.point: According to the Geophysical Institute of Peru (IGP), the epicentre was located 30 km northwest of Junín, at a depth of more than 129 km; the US Geological Survey (USGS) puts it at 108 km [2][4].
The civil defence agency (Indeci) reports a cracked hospital in Pichanaqui, in the Junín region, a collapsed house wall and power cuts in at least two towns [2].
Landslides and rockfalls were observed on mountainsides; in Lima, residents left their homes [1][3].
No tsunami warning was issued and no injuries had been reported in the first few hours [1][2].
news.2026-11-21-perou-seisme-junin.why.0: Key takeaway: despite its magnitude, this deep earthquake caused only limited damage according to initial reports, with no casualties reported [1][2][4].
news.2026-11-21-perou-seisme-junin.why.1: The assessments remain provisional: rockslides on mountain roads and a cracked hospital in Pichanaqui show the fragility of Andean infrastructure, which the civil defence agency is still inspecting [1][2].
news.2026-11-21-perou-seisme-junin.forMe: If you have a trip planned to Peru, particularly in the central Andes, check road conditions: rockslides have been reported. Otherwise, there is no direct effect on your daily life.

news.2026-11-21-indonesie-chine-accord-e: Indonesia: Prabowo and Xi launch negotiations on a major economic agreement and sign 35 contracts worth $15 billion

On Friday, November 20, in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of APEC, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto and Chinese President Xi Jinping announced the launch of negotiations on a comprehensive economic partnership agreement between their two countries. A business forum produced 35 contracts worth about $15 billion [1][2][3].
Xi Jinping wants a “comprehensive and high-level” agreement, concluded quickly, and wants to deepen cooperation on the Jakarta-Bandung high-speed railway, energy, minerals and AI [1][2].
Prabowo Subianto said the strategic partnership with China was “stronger than ever” and promised Chinese investors a “stable and predictable” business climate [1][4].
According to Prabowo's office, the 35 contracts signed in Shenzhen, worth about $15 billion, cover data centres and renewable energy in particular [3].
The two leaders also discussed cooperation in the South China Sea, including possible joint development zones, a sensitive subject since the controversy over a maritime agreement signed in 2024 [3].
Key takeaway: Indonesia wants to cement its ties with Beijing in a comprehensive agreement, but the negotiations do not yet have a published timetable or content [1][3].
The opening of talks on joint zones in the South China Sea is a cause for concern, as it may be seen as a concession to Chinese claims in an area disputed by several countries in the region [3].
This rapprochement plays out in minerals, energy and digital technology, sectors in which Europe is also looking for partners to reduce its dependence on China.

news.2026-11-21-liban-frappe-israel-beka: Lebanon: Israel strikes a site in the Bekaa where Hezbollah was allegedly rebuilding missiles, as the disarmament plan stalls

On Thursday, November 19, the Israeli army struck a site in the Bekaa Valley, in eastern Lebanon, which it describes as a missile factory and weapons depot being rebuilt by Hezbollah. No casualties were reported [1][2].
According to Israel, Hezbollah was trying to bring this site back into service as a missile production and weapons storage facility. The Shiite movement did not react immediately [1][2].
A few days earlier, Israel said it had targeted a weapons shipment for Hezbollah near the Syrian border [1].

The last war between Israel and Hezbollah ended with a ceasefire brokered by Washington on June 20, but the Israeli army occupies dozens of villages in the south, in a “security zone” about 10 km deep [2].
The US plan provides for Hezbollah's disarmament, a gradual Israeli withdrawal and the deployment of the Lebanese army in the south; it is blocked, as Hezbollah refuses to give up its weapons [2].
Key takeaway: even after the ceasefire, Israel keeps striking Lebanon whenever it suspects Hezbollah of rearming, and the US peace plan is not moving forward [1][2].

The deadline is approaching: the mandate of UNIFIL, the UN force in southern Lebanon, ends at the end of 2026 [2]. Hezbollah, weakened by two wars since 2023, dragged Lebanon into the regional conflict in March by firing rockets at Israel [2].
The end of UNIFIL, in a few weeks, raises the question of who will monitor the border, and therefore the risk of a new war in a country close to France.
